description: Two students from Sorocaba, Brazil (Computer Engineering and Data Science) who love hackathons and competitions. Bruna brings backend, competitive programming and 3D (Three.js, Blender); Eduardo brings statistics, data analysis and AI in Python. We like work that is rigorous and visually clear. Looking for: UI/UX or front-end, ML or remote sensing, Earth science or astronomy. Curiosity over experience.
summary: Astro Romana is a cooperative browser game, designed for a crew of up to four, about designing and flying a science mission to Mars. The mission is split into four roles, each owning part of its resources: Helena (commander: mass, launch, budget), Lucas (systems: power, lifetime), Oscar (telecom: data, communications) and Maya (science: instruments, crew). Roles without a player are taken by AI crewmates. The team assembles a modular rocket from real engines and tanks (Merlin, RL10, Raptor, RS-25…), and the builder checks thrust-to-weight, staged Δv, power and cost as they go, so every part has a consequence. Then they fly it: liftoff, docking, orbital refuelling, and a landing that follows Perseverance's real entry profile onto real HiRISE terrain of Gale or Jezero crater. On the surface, each crew member plays a minigame based on a real experiment (MOXIE, PIXL/SHERLOC, UHF relay, rover route scouting) whose result affects the others. Failures explain why they happened, and "Real fact" cards tell what happened on the actual mission. Even the soundtrack is generated from Curiosity's radiation measurements. The game turns trade-offs that are usually taught only in theory into decisions students feel, argue about and retry as a team.
details:
WHAT IS IT

Astro Romana is a cooperative browser game, designed for a crew of up to four, that takes a science mission to Mars from concept to operation. Each of the four roles owns part of the mission's resources: Helena (commander: mass, launch vehicle, budget), Lucas (systems: power, lifetime), Oscar (telecom: data, communications) and Maya (science: instruments, crew health). AI crewmates take any role without a player.

HOW IT WORKS

Plan. On a 3D solar system the crew picks Mars, a landing site (Jezero or Gale crater, shown in real HiRISE photos) and a difficulty level.

Design. The team builds the rocket from 55 parts based on real hardware, from Merlin, RL10, RS-25 and Raptor engines to PIXL/SHERLOC instruments, Electra and DSOC radios, ROSA solar arrays and a storm shelter. Live telemetry shows mass, thrust-to-weight, Δv per stage, power, and cost against budget, so every module that adds science also adds mass, power draw and cost.

Fly. After the countdown, the crew flies four timed stages from an Orion-style cockpit: liftoff, cabin docking, refuelling in orbit, and a landing that follows Perseverance's real entry profile. Every member has a job, and design choices show up in flight: a heavy rocket wallows, fins damp the gusts, a power deficit throws sparks, and a rocket without enough Δv aborts into the ocean.

Explore. The crew walks on 3D terrain built from real HiRISE elevation data around the Perseverance and Curiosity landing points. Each member runs an experiment based on a real one (rover route scouting, MOXIE oxygen, UHF relay, PIXL/SHERLOC biosignatures), which ends with a "Real fact" card. Anyone not back at the lander in time is left behind.

Debrief. The game scores the mission, ranks the crew and explains every result, so the team can redesign and fly again.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Mission trade-offs are usually taught in theory. In Astro Romana they become decisions the team argues about and then feels in flight, and replaying shows that there is rarely one perfect design. The game runs in any browser, on a computer or a phone, with no install, and three difficulty levels serve beginners and advanced players alike, so it fits classrooms and outreach events.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

Game: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with three.js; no build step, it even runs from local files.

Assets generated by code in Node.js: crew avatars with a shared rig and animations, 55 rocket parts and a low-poly Earth coloured from MODIS, ETOPO1 and AMSR2 data, checked with the Khronos glTF Validator.

Real Mars terrain: HiRISE elevation models and images read with geotiff.js from the USGS STAC catalog, plus a 100 km horizon from CTX and MOLA–HRSC.

Soundtrack: generated from Curiosity's RAD radiation data, in plain JavaScript.

Room server: WebSocket (Node.js and ws) on a Google Cloud VM with Caddy.

AI: Claude Code as a coding assistant; the team checked every result and number against the sources.

Data: NASA (MRO, MGS, MSL, GIBS, NSSDC, JPL), ESA, USGS, NOAA and the user guides of real engines and tanks, all credited in our references.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Real ground: players walk where Perseverance and Curiosity landed, on terrain measured from orbit.

The soundtrack is data: four quiet Martian days and the May 2024 solar storm, when radiation at Gale crater rose about 79-fold in under an hour, turned into sound.

A launch from home: the launch pad stands in a low-poly version of the Sorocaba Technology Park, so the mission leaves from home.

One style: the interface and the 3D models share one faceted low-poly style, all generated by code.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accuracy and fun: every number shown as real has a source, and gameplay values are marked as such. Of the 21 experiment minigames we designed from real missions, 4 made it into this version.

Accessibility: phone and desktop widths, reduced motion, 2D fallbacks, mouse, touch and keyboard, and plain English that explains why a decision matters.

Licensing: only open data and images, with credits; no agency logos.

Team play: the score drops for anyone left behind, so the crew wins or loses together.
